title: Land a hoisted motor on its base's four studs: one hand runs the hoist, the other steers the load
instruction: Set the motor down on its base with the hoist, all four feet over the base's studs and flat on the base, and leave the hoist chain slack. Let go of the motor and the pendant when you are done.
context: Hand laborers and material movers hook loads to hoists and guide them into place (O*NET 53-7062: "Attach slings, hooks, or other devices to lift cargo and guide loads"; "Adjust controls to guide, position, or move equipment, such as cranes"); maintenance workers refit motors on their bases (49-9071). A shop chain hoist runs only while DOWN is held and its hook rarely hangs exactly over the seat, so one hand holds the button while the other pulls the hanging load against the pendulum's pull, squares it and keeps it over the studs as it comes down. Hoist practice (ASME B30.16, OSHA 1910.179) keeps hands out from under a suspended load and out of the gap between a load and its seat. Unlike setting a lifted plate down and switching off a hand-carried lifting magnet, one hand runs a hold-to-run hoist while the other steers the swinging load onto 0.4 mm-clearance studs; unlike damping a hanging load or hoisting a bucket onto a deck, the test is landing a heavy part on a fastener pattern.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left, z up from the table top). Motor base: a fixed grey steel plate 26 (x) x 20 (y) x 1.2 cm centred at x 30, y 0, with four 3/8-16 steel studs (9.5 mm) standing 3.8 cm proud of it at x 20.5 / 39.5, y -5.7 / +5.7 (the NEMA 182T foot pattern, 19.05 x 11.43 cm), each tip chamfered 3 mm x 45 deg. Motor: a 3 hp TEFC NEMA 182T motor, 33 kg, finned frame 22 cm across, 38 cm long from fan cover to the 1-1/8 in keyed shaft, axis along y with the shaft toward -y; four cast feet 4.5 x 4.5 x 1.2 cm, each with a 10.3 mm (13/32 in) hole (square 10.3 mm in the model; studs octagonal 9.5 mm across flats, 0.4 mm minimum clearance), shaft axis 11.43 cm above the foot undersides; a cast conduit box 7 x 7 x 6 cm on the -x side (toward the arms), centred about 16 cm above the table at the start; a forged eyebolt on top over the centre of mass. Hoist: a 1/4-ton electric chain hoist on a gantry above the cameras' view, run on its slow speed of 2.0 cm/s (two-speed hoist, as used for landing loads); its chain runs 85 cm from the hook to the eyebolt (1.00 m hook to centre of mass), and the hook has a free swivel. At the start the motor hangs still with its foot undersides 6.0 cm above the stud tips, its hole pattern 1.0 cm toward the arms (-x) and 0.5 cm left (+y) of the studs and turned 6 deg about vertical (the hook's parked position; the trolley is clamped at its parking stop for the trial). Pendant: a black two-button pendant 20 x 6 x 4 cm lying on its back in a fixed cradle 22 x 8 x 6 cm at x 20, y -25, buttons facing up, tops 11 cm above the table: green 22 mm DOWN at x 17, black UP at x 23. Each button travels 4 mm on a spring (about 6 N at full travel); the hoist runs only while a button is held down at least 2.5 mm. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: From the episode's recorded poses (on a real rig: the three trial videos, a feeler gauge under each foot and a tape on the chain). Whole-trial zero gates, latched (putting things right afterwards does not undo them): (1) under the load: any part of the robot below the motor's lowest point inside its plan outline grown by 1 cm, at any time before all four feet are down on the plate; (2) pinch: any part of the robot between a foot and the plate while that foot's underside is less than 5 cm above the plate; (3) stud strike: a foot touches a stud while moving faster than 5 cm/s. A stud is through when its hole's centre is within 3 mm of it seen from above and the foot's underside is below the stud's tip; flat is every foot underside within 1 mm of the plate; slack is the chain at least 1 cm longer than the hook-to-eyebolt distance. Read at the last step: 1.0 all four studs through, flat, chain slack by 1 to 15 cm, both grippers at least 5 cm from the motor, both buttons up and the motor still, held 1 s; 0.75 all four through and flat but not all of that (chain still taut, a button still held, a gripper within 5 cm, chain run out more than 15 cm onto the motor, or still moving); 0.5 load off the hoist (chain at least 5 mm slack) with two or more studs through. Latched from any time in the episode: 0.25 all four holes were within 3 mm of their studs seen from above with the feet less than 1 cm above the stud tips (low side views). Else 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Real trial safety: a 1/4-ton electric chain hoist with upper and lower limit switches and a pendant emergency stop, on a gantry rated at least 500 kg; the operator holds an emergency stop that cuts both the hoist and the robot, and the trial is aborted the moment the under-load gate fires. Reset: press UP until the foot undersides are 6.0 cm above the stud tips (tape from the plate); unclamp, push the hook trolley back to its marked parking stop and clamp it, checked with a plumb bob from the eyebolt to marks on the plate (1.0 cm -x, 0.5 cm +y, within 2 mm); turn the motor to the 6 deg mark against a yaw stop on a tag line (6 +- 1 deg; the free swivel has no restoring torque), then free the tag line and let the swing die below 2 mm.
fidelity: Rigid bodies (PhysX, 240 Hz) built from boxes at real NEMA 182T dimensions (feet, holes, studs, eyebolt, conduit box) and real mass. The chain is a D6 joint with only a distance limit (85 cm, goes slack) from a hook block that moves at 2.0 cm/s only while a spring button on the pendant is pressed 2.5 mm; the swivel is free. Studs are octagons with chamfered tips in square holes, 0.4 mm clearance; steel on steel mu 0.25. The pendant lies in a cradle, not on its cable.
